frames.title: Clinic note (AI draft for clinician review)

history: Lives with family and is independent in daily activities.
Works in an office and walks for 30 minutes most days.
Family history of type 2 diabetes in the mother.
Up to date with routine vaccinations.
exam: Heart sounds dual with no added sounds; chest clear on auscultation.
Abdomen soft and non-tender with no organomegaly.
Weight stable compared with the last visit.
vitals: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 76/min, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on air, temperature 36.8 C.
BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 70/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on air, temperature 36.6 C.

plan: Results and plan discussed with the patient, who agrees.
Letter to the GP to follow.
admin: History obtained from the patient and an accompanying relative.
Interpreter not required; consultation conducted in English.
Consent obtained for examination; chaperone offered.
Previous records reviewed on the electronic health record.
Note drafted from the consultation transcript for clinician review.

lines: Doctor: Have you had any thoughts that life is not worth living?
Patient: Sometimes, over the last {duration}, I've wished I could go to sleep and not wake up. I haven't made any plans.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. We'll talk about support today.
Patient: I'll be honest, I've thought about taking all my {med} tablets.
Doctor: Have you made any plans or taken any steps towards that?
Patient: I counted them {when}, but I didn't take any.
Doctor: I'm glad you told me. I'd like the crisis team to see you today, and we'll keep you safe.
Doctor: Any previous hospital admissions?
Patient: {years} ago I took about {n} paracetamol tablets after a break-up. I was in hospital for {days} days on a drip.
Doctor: Okay, I'll note that history of overdose.
Doctor: Do you have access to anything you could use to harm yourself, like stored medicines or {means}?
Patient: There's {means} at home, my husband keeps it.
Doctor: Could someone remove that from the house for now? That's an important part of keeping you safe.
Patient: I've been cutting my {site} again when things get too much.
Doctor: When was the last time?
Patient: {when}. They're not deep.
Doctor: Can I have a look at them? Let's dress them and talk about other ways to cope.
Doctor: How did you get these bruises on your {site}?
Patient: My partner {act} when he's been drinking. It's been happening for {duration}.
Doctor: That must be very frightening. You're not to blame. Would you like to talk to our domestic abuse advocate today?
Patient: I've never told anyone, but my {relative} sexually abused me when I was {age}.
Doctor: Thank you for trusting me with that. How is it affecting you now?
Patient: I have nightmares and I can't be touched without panicking.
Patient: My {relative} takes my pension and shouts at me if I ask for it. Last month {pronoun} locked me in my room.
Doctor: I'm concerned about your safety. With your permission, I'd like to involve the adult safeguarding team.
Patient: I was {act} outside a pub on {day}.
Doctor: Did you lose consciousness? Where were you hurt?
Patient: I got {injury}. The police have taken a statement.
Doctor: How much do you drink in a typical day?
Patient: About {amount} most days, more at weekends.
Doctor: Do you ever get shaky in the morning or need a drink to settle your nerves?
Patient: {answer}

answer: Yes, I shake until I have one.
